quote: and realized that I had overestimated the difficulty of almost every single important problem.
content: Two problems. First, the best-established finding about how people estimate difficulty is the opposite: they underestimate how long and how hard their own projects will be (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994). Second, the sample is selected. The “important problems” counted are the ones that became tractable to the author; the central one — a provably Friendly AI, which the essay says became “merely extremely difficult” — was not solved, and in 2022 the author published “MIRI announces new ‘Death With Dignity’ strategy” — on April Fools' Day, and explicitly not as a joke — concluding that the problem would probably not be solved in time. By the essay's own principal test case, the difficulty was not overestimated.

quote: Richard Hamming used to go around asking his fellow scientists two questions: “What are the important problems in your field?,” and, “Why aren’t you working on them?”
content: Hamming defined the phrase, in the same talk (“You and Your Research,” 1986), in a way that excludes this essay's use of it. He said that he and his colleagues did not work on time travel, teleportation or antigravity, and that these were not important problems, “because we do not have an attack”; importance, for Hamming, meant a problem whose solution would matter and for which there was a reasonable line of attack. The essay borrows his authority for the opposite claim — that “not uncommonly, the most important problems in your field are impossible.” For Hamming, a problem without an attack was the very thing you should not be working on.

quote: That’s why you don’t see more philosophers working on reductionist decompositions of consciousness.
content: You see many. Reductive and functionalist accounts of consciousness are a large literature — Dennett, the Churchlands, higher-order theories, global workspace theory — and the empirical programmes descended from them are now tested head-to-head: the preregistered adversarial collaboration between global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory published its results in Nature (Cogitate Consortium, 2025), with each theory failing some of its own predictions. That is what working on the “impossible” problem looks like when a field does it. The sentence mistakes the author's not having read the literature for its absence.

quote: And I realized that the word “impossible” had two usages:
content: A useful distinction as far as it goes, but the list omits the categories that most often matter. A problem can be possible in principle and computationally intractable (NP-hard, or undecidable in general, as Rice's theorem makes most interesting program properties); possible and infeasible with any resources that will exist in time; or impossible in its stated form because the specification is inconsistent, as Arrow's theorem shows for some demands on aggregating preferences — the kind of demand an AI meant to act on “humanity's values” makes. The essay's dichotomy makes every non-proof “impossible” a failure of nerve; the missing categories are where most sensible judgments of impossibility live.
